name: Gareth Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Gareth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't campaign for anything. What you say is confidential and won't have your name on it. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Depends on the weather, really. I'm a senior lineman on the coast, and on a calm day we're replacing old poles that the salt air has eaten, or swapping out insulators. When a storm comes in, that's my real job: I lead the restoration crew, and we go out in the dark and the wind and get people back on. I've done thirty-hour stretches. What I like is the moment the lights come back on in a street and people come out and wave.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The office side of it. They gave us tablets two years ago and I still fill in my sheets on paper and let the supervisor type them up. My wife Helen says I'm a dinosaur, and she works in the office at a builders' merchant, so she knows about computers. I just don't see the point when I can do it faster with a pen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go. I wouldn't post anything, I'm not on any of that. At work I'd just say the storms still come and somebody still has to go out in them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means things stay as they are, and that suits me fine. I've got a good job, the pay's steady, and we're slowly getting the mortgage down. I'd just keep my head down and keep working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Exactly what I'm doing now. Go to work, do the storm rota, take the overtime when it comes. Maybe finally fix the back fence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Calm. Nothing to worry about there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep your head down. Is there anything at work you'd want to change, if nothing big happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get rid of the tablets, if I'm honest. Stuart, who's been my second on the crew for twelve years, feels the same. We lost twenty minutes on a job last month because the screen froze in the cold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the overtime pay for in your house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom's football boots, Ella's swimming, the odd week at the caravan. Storm season pays for summer, that's how Helen puts it. Without it we'd be tight but okay.

S0.say: I'd just say the storms still come and somebody has to go out in them. I wouldn't post anything because I'm not on social media.
S0.think: I think things stay as they are, and that suits me. Good job, steady pay and the mortgage slowly coming down.
S0.do: Carries on exactly as now, working the storm rota and taking overtime. Plans small jobs at home like fixing the back fence.
S0.feel: Calm, with nothing to worry about.
S0.quote: Storm season pays for summer, that's how Helen puts it.
S0.fieldNote: Gareth is content and wants nothing to change, including getting rid of the tablets he already resents. Storm overtime is a real part of the family budget. He talks about his work with quiet pride, especially the lights coming back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not going to do much to us. Maybe in offices, but they're not going to send a computer up a pole in a gale. That's what I'd say to the lads, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truth is, I think it'd mostly pass me by. Maybe they'd fly drones along the lines and we'd do fewer patrols. But in a storm you need people who know the network, and I know this coast better than anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I'd wait and see what the company actually does before I changed anything. If they made me learn something new, I'd do it, but I wouldn't go looking for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Maybe a little bit wary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said in a storm you need people who know the network. What does knowing it mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I know that the pole at the bottom of Harbour Lane leans in a south-westerly, and the line up to the lighthouse cottages always trips first. That's not written down anywhere. It's in my head and Stuart's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the company wanted to write that knowledge down, maybe into a computer system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They've tried. A young engineer came round with a laptop asking questions last year. I told him some of it, but you can't put feel into a laptop.

S1.say: I'd say it won't do much to us. They're not going to send a computer up a pole in a gale.
S1.think: I think it mostly passes me by, maybe with some drone patrols. In a storm you still need people who know the coast, and I know it best.
S1.do: Waits to see what the company actually does before changing anything. Would learn something new only if made to, and keeps working as normal.
S1.quote: That's not written down anywhere. It's in my head and Stuart's.
S1.fieldNote: His confidence rests on local knowledge that isn't written down. He's guarded about sharing it with the company, perhaps without fully seeing why. He sees no reason to act until change is in front of him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what I'd say. Probably that someone needs to sort it out, the government or the company or whoever. I'm not one for speeches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it'd scare me. I've no other trade, I'm not good with computers, and I'm forty-three. If a robot can climb in a storm and does it cheaper, I'm done. We've got maybe five months of money if we're careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, the caravan goes, we'd sell it. Helen and I would cut everything back and try to get the savings up while I've still got the job. I'd find out what the redundancy is, and if it came to it I'd ask my dad if we could stay with him for a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, really. I don't like thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about learning something new in those two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to say yes. But I've seen myself with that tablet, and I know how long it takes me. Two years wouldn't be enough for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tom, who's fifteen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him not to follow me into the lines. He was talking about an apprenticeship next year. I'd have to tell him to think again, and I'd hate that.

S2.say: I don't know what I'd say, probably that someone needs to sort it out, the government or the company. I'm not one for speeches.
S2.think: I think it would finish me: no other trade, not good with computers, forty-three and about five months of money if we're careful.
S2.do: Sells the caravan and cuts back spending to build savings while still employed. Checks redundancy terms and asks his father about staying with him if needed.
S2.quote: If a robot can climb in a storm and does it cheaper, I'm done.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture breaks his core belief that storm work is safe. He's honest that he couldn't learn fast enough, which was hard for him to say. He doesn't have a clear person to blame, which fits his centre outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to plan, so the company and the government had better plan. People like me shouldn't just be dropped. That's about as political as I get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'd keep hoping it doesn't really happen to storm work. But I'd know it probably would. I'd be forty-eight, and that's young enough to be in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put every bit of overtime into savings, not the caravan. We'd keep the cars going longer instead of changing them. And I'd watch to see whether the robots actually work out here on the coast before I did anything bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A sort of knot that sits there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd watch to see whether the robots work. What would you need to see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need to see one go up a wet pole at night with the wind coming off the sea. If I saw that, I'd believe it. Until then, it's people in offices telling me what my job is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you saw it in year two, what would you do then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have to think about something else, maybe driving or warehouse work. I don't know. I'd probably talk to Stuart first, he's better at this stuff than me.

S3.say: I'd say there's time to plan, so the company and government had better plan. People like me shouldn't just be dropped.
S3.think: I think I'd keep hoping storm work is spared but know it probably isn't. At forty-eight, I'd be young enough to be in trouble.
S3.do: Puts all overtime into savings and keeps the cars longer. Waits to see robots working on the coast before doing anything bigger.
S3.quote: Until then, it's people in offices telling me what my job is.
S3.fieldNote: Five years softens the shock but he still waits rather than acts. He needs to see a robot in real coastal weather before he'll believe it. His fallback ideas, driving or warehouse work, are vague and could themselves be automated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the last one. There's plenty of time, so sort it out properly. Don't leave older workers on the scrap heap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be fifty-three. I'd hope I could get close enough to the end that it doesn't matter as much. The kids would be grown, and the mortgage would be smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not much, at first. I'd keep saving, keep working. I'd wait and see how it goes over the first few years before deciding anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's far off. I can put it to the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fifty-three isn't retirement age, though. What happens between then and your pension?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit I don't like to think about. Maybe I'd find something, maybe I wouldn't. Helen would probably make me sit down and plan it, she's the planner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having ten years make you more likely to learn something new, or less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less, if I'm honest. Ten years feels like long enough to wait. I know that's probably the wrong answer.

S4.say: I'd say there's plenty of time, so sort it out properly. Don't leave older workers on the scrap heap.
S4.think: I think at fifty-three I'd be close enough to the end that it matters less. The kids would be grown and the mortgage smaller.
S4.do: Keeps saving and working without changing anything at first. Waits to see how the first few years go before deciding.
S4.feel: Uneasy but able to push it to the back of his mind.
S4.quote: Ten years feels like long enough to wait.
S4.fieldNote: More warning time makes him less likely to act, which he admits is probably the wrong answer. He leans on his wife as the planner. The gap between fifty-three and pension age is clearly something he avoids thinking about.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is a decent payout, enough to clear a good chunk of the mortgage, and somebody actually helping men like me find the next thing, not just a website. Someone who'll sit down with you.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not against progress. I'm just not convinced. When the lights go off in a storm, nobody rings a robot, they ring us.

headlineQuote: When the lights go off in a storm, nobody rings a robot, they ring us.
portrait: Gareth Alvarez is a 43-year-old senior lineman who leads storm restoration on a coastal network and still fills in his job sheets on paper. He's content with life as it is and believes local knowledge and storm work keep him safe. Steady change barely worries him. The two-year AGI picture alarms him because he has no other trade, is slow with computers and has about five months of savings. More warning time makes him wait rather than act, and he admits that ten years feels like long enough to put off deciding.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd have no other trade to fall back on and only a few months of savings.
whatWouldHelp: A payout big enough to clear a good chunk of the mortgage, and a real person to help him find his next job.
